papers.title: Local sleep in wake is widespread across the rat cortex and tracks sleep need
papers.abstract: During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, cortical neurons alternate between ON periods of firing and OFF periods of silence, the latter accounting for the slow waves of the EEG. Converging evidence indicates that OFF periods can also occur locally during extended wake ("local sleep"), at a behavioral cost, but whether this phenomenon is ubiquitous across the cortex, whether some areas are more resilient than others, and whether it can also provide any benefit, remain open questions. Here we recorded from 11 cortical areas (and claustrum) in 15 rats using high-density Neuropixels probes and detected OFF periods with a novel method that captures spatially restricted and irregularly shaped events mischaracterized or missed by traditional methods. We found OFF periods during extended wake in every region tested, with no evidence that any area is spared. Over the course of sleep deprivation, OFF periods became more frequent, longer, larger, and quieter, and their features correlated with delta power on a per-event basis in both wake and NREM sleep, consistent with the notion that they reflect accumulating sleep need. The extent to which OFF periods overlapped across areas also increased across sleep deprivation. Finally, the rate of medium and large OFF periods during sleep deprivation was negatively correlated with their rebound in subsequent recovery sleep, consistent with the possibility that local sleep in wake partially discharges sleep need before the animal falls asleep. Statement of SignificanceProlonged wakefulness drives small groups of cortical neurons into brief sleep-like states even as the animal remains awake and behaving. This "local sleep" in wake is thought to underlie the errors and slowed responses of sleep deprivation, but how widespread it is, and whether it helps, remains unclear. Using high-density recordings across many cortical regions in the rat and a novel detection method sensitive to small, irregular events, we show that local sleep is not confined to a few vulnerable areas but occurs throughout the cortex, growing with accumulating sleep need. We also find that these neuronal lapses may begin to relieve that need before sleep takes over, suggesting that they may represent an early, piecemeal form of recovery.

papers.title: Melatonin increases NREM sleep duration in aged rats alongside changes in choroid plexus SIRT3 and cerebrospinal fluid calcium.
papers.abstract: The relationship between age-related sleep disruption, choroid plexus (ChP) proteins, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) calcium remains unclear. Male rats aged 1, 3, and 18 months were assessed using 24-h electroencephalography/electromyography, ex vivo current-clamp recordings, calcium assays, and ChP immunoblotting. In aged rats, melatonin, melatonin plus 3-TYP, and alpha-lipoic acid were evaluated in 14-day treatment comparisons. Cortical responses to altered extracellular calcium were assessed separately. Older rats exhibited more fragmented sleep, reduced non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, reduced cortical and ventrolateral preoptic neuronal firing under identical recording conditions, and lower ChP sirtuin 3 (SIRT3) and combined ATP2B1/2/3 immunoreactivity. CSF calcium did not differ significantly between the 3- and 18-month-old groups. Lowering extracellular calcium increased cortical firing, whereas raising it reduced firing. Melatonin increased total and NREM sleep time, CSF and plasma calcium, and ChP SIRT3 and combined ATP2B1/2/3 immunoreactivity, without significantly changing total REM sleep. Compared with melatonin alone, 3-TYP co-treatment reduced total, NREM, and REM sleep duration and attenuated selected biochemical responses. Alpha-lipoic acid partially reproduced the melatonin-associated pattern. Within-group Pearson analyses identified positive associations between CSF calcium and total sleep time in all three age groups and all four treatment groups after Holm-Šídák adjustment. These findings show that melatonin-associated increases in total sleep time accompany changes in ChP proteins and CSF calcium in aged rats, providing a basis for testing whether the ChP-CSF interface contributes to sleep regulation.

papers.title: A Temporally Causal Two-Layer Framework for Wearable EEG Sleep Staging and Short-Horizon Sleep-Transition Forecasting.
papers.abstract: Reliable online sleep monitoring requires sleep-stage estimates and forecasts based only on information available at the time of prediction. This study developed a temporally causal two-layer framework for wearable electroencephalography (EEG) sleep staging and short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting. Using 128 Bitbrain Open Access Sleep (BOAS) recordings from 100 participants, the first layer (M0) performed five-stage sleep classification with causal signal processing and participant-isolated nested validation. The second layer (M1) used strictly cross-fitted histories of M0 stage probabilities to predict transitions from wake or N1 (W/N1) to N2, N3, or REM sleep (N2+) within 60, 90, or 120 s after each observed 30-s epoch. M1 eligibility was determined from M0-predicted stages during training and evaluation, without requiring polysomnography (PSG) stage labels at inference. M0 achieved 0.830 accuracy and 0.704 macro-F1. Under M0-predicted eligibility, M1 achieved AUROC values of 0.801, 0.791, and 0.786 at 60, 90, and 120 s, respectively; complementary PSG-conditioned evaluation yielded 0.814, 0.803, and 0.801. Prediction was stronger during wakefulness than N1, and the benefits of probability history were specific to the future-sleep task. Future-perturbation tests confirmed unchanged pre-boundary outputs under the tested conditions. A frozen M0 replay on three Muse S Gen2 nights further identified stage-specific limitations in cross-device transfer. These findings establish an auditable framework for temporally causal wearable EEG analysis and demonstrate the potential of short-horizon sleep-transition forecasting while identifying its current generalization boundaries.

papers.title: RXFP1 alleviates chronic sleep fragmentation-induced cognitive impairment by suppressing microglia activation-mediated neuroinflammation.
papers.abstract: Chronic sleep fragmentation (CSF) poses a serious threat to physical and mental health and leads to the cognitive decline. Behavioral tests revealed that learning and memory functions were impaired in CSF mice. Transcriptomic analysis was performed on hippocampal tissues from CSF mice, and the results indicated that DEGs were predominantly enriched in CSF-related pathways including behavior, circadian rhythms, inflammation, and neuronal functions. Relaxin family peptide receptor 1 (RXFP1) gene was identified for further investigation. In the hippocampus of CSF mice, mRNA levels of RXFP1 were decreased. CSF mice receiving intrahippocampal AAV9-RXFP1 exhibited better performance in the Morris water maze and object location recognition tests RXFP1 overexpression ameliorated hippocampal damage, neuronal loss, and apoptosis in CSF mice. RXFP1 overexpression suppressed microglial activation in the hippocampal region of CSF mice, reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and down-regulated the mRNA expression of PTGS2 and NOS2. Furthermore, iNOS expression was decreased in microglia isolated from the hippocampus of CSF mice receiving intrahippocampal AAV9-RXFP1. RXFP1 overexpression inhibited the expression of TLR4 and MyD88 in the hippocampus of CSF mice, and reduced nuclear translocation of p65 in both hippocampal tissue and microglia. RXFP1 overexpression suppressed LPS-induced activation of BV2 cells and blocked the NF-κB signaling pathway. Rescue experiments confirmed that RXFP1 modulates microglial activation via the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling cascade. The present study demonstrated that RXFP1 might alleviate cognitive impairment in CSF mice, at least in part, by suppressing microglia-associated neuroinflammation and the downstream TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway.

papers.title: Dihydromyricetin Regulates Sleep and Protects Against Oxidative Stress in Drosophila melanogaster.
papers.abstract: Sleep homeostasis is essential for health, and sleep disturbances contribute to multi-organ failure mortality. Dihydromyricetin (DMY), a flavonoid from Ampelopsis grossedentata, possesses anti-inflammatory and antioxidant activities. Although DMY alleviates sleep-deprivation-induced cognitive deficits, its role in sleep regulation remains unclear. Here, we show that DMY increases sleep duration and modulates sleep fragmentation in young, aged, and short-sleep mutant Drosophila. Transcriptomic and genetic analyses reveal that DMY alters the expression of neurotransmitter-related genes, including VGAT and Trhn, suggesting potential involvement of GABAergic and serotonergic signaling. In paraquat-induced oxidative stress models, DMY boosts antioxidant gene expression, alleviates oxidative damage and intestinal apoptosis, restores stress-disrupted sleep, and extends lifespan. Together, our findings demonstrate that DMY improves sleep-associated parameters, potentially involving neurotransmitter-related signaling pathways while concurrently mitigating oxidative stress-induced damage, thereby promoting organismal health and suggesting its potential for preventing and treating sleep disorders and aging-related decline.

papers.title: Environmental Enrichment and Operant Behavior: A Review of Insights from Animal Research for Clinical Applications.
papers.abstract: In recent years, environmental enrichment (EE) has increasingly been incorporated into the housing conditions of laboratory animals as it influences animal behavior and brain function. Differences in housing conditions represent a critical challenge, that potentially compromises the reproducibility of experimental results. Furthermore, findings related to EE are expected to contribute to the treatment of mental health disorders and prevention of relapse. However, a comprehensive overview of the effects of EE on operant learning, particularly on lever pressing, is currently lacking. In this review, we compiled and summarized previous studies that investigated the effects of EE on lever pressing during operant learning in rats and mice. When food served as a reward, EE influenced exploratory behavior and learning but exerted little effect on motivation to get a reward and behavioral flexibility in response to a task paradigm shift. In contrast when sucrose was used, EE suppressed motivation and, depending on the experimental model, exerted contrasting effects by either enhancing or inhibiting exploratory behavior. Finally, when addictive drugs were used, EE generally suppressed drug self-administration and relapse-related behaviors. Collectively, these findings suggest that EE modulates operant learning behavior in a manner dependent upon both the type of reward and the experimental conditions.

papers.title: Pre-anaesthetic anxiety phenotype stratifies anaesthesia EEG, acquired navigation, and post-anaesthesia sleep in sevoflurane-exposed mice
papers.abstract: Preoperative anxiety is common and has been associated with postoperative delirium, yet whether an anxious phenotype changes the brain's response to anaesthesia is unknown. Here, 42 mice are classified as low-anxiety (LA) or high-anxiety (HA) by fear-retrieval freezing and exposed to sevoflurane without surgery. When adequate anaesthetic effects are reached, HA mice show a higher aperiodic spectral edge frequency than LA mice. After anaesthesia, both groups retain choice accuracy in the Water Cross Maze, but in the same trials decomposed into behavioural syllables, the learned navigation sequence is selectively disrupted in HA mice. Rapid eye-movement sleep decreases in HA mice and increases in LA mice. A single anxiety phenotype defined before induction therefore tracks three responses to the same sevoflurane exposure. These findings suggest that pre-anaesthetic anxiety marks individual vulnerability to anaesthesia in mice. The results may pave the way to interventions preserving cognitive function and sleep during perioperative recovery.

papers.title: Housing environmental enrichment influences mouse behavior and response to experimental metabolic disorders.
papers.abstract: Housing environmental is essential for animal welfare but may also influence the metabolic and behavioral outcomes of preclinical studies. This study investigates whether two commonly used enrichment materials, Nestlets and Sizzle, modify the effects of a high-fat diet (HFD) on metabolic and behavioral phenotypes in adult male C57BL/6 J mice. A total of 128 mice were fed either a normal diet (ND) or HFD for six months and housed in enriched cages containing either Nestlets (Nest) or Sizzle nesting material (n = 32 mice/condition). Metabolic parameters and behavioral performances were assessed at six months. Results show that HFD induced weight gain, hypercholesterolemia, fasting hyperglycemia, and impaired glucose tolerance under both enrichment conditions. However, Nest-enriched mice displayed lower cholesterol levels and differences in glycemic responses compared with Sizzle-enriched mice, suggesting that nesting material can modulate the severity of diet-induced metabolic alterations. Furthermore, environmental housing also affected behavior. Nest-enriched mice showed higher locomotor activity and reduced anxiety compared with Sizzle-enriched mice. Interestingly, HFD-induced impairment of visual recognition memory in the novel object recognition test was detected only in Nest-enriched mice. Overall, these findings demonstrate that different enrichment materials can substantially modify metabolic, emotional, motivational, and cognitive responses to HFD. These results highlight the need to carefully control and consistently maintain housing environmental conditions throughout long-term preclinical studies to improve reproducibility, interpretation of behavioral outcomes, and animal welfare.

papers.title: Phox2b 25-Ala expansion leads to Congenital Central Hypoventilation Syndrome like phenotypes in mice.
papers.abstract: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is a rare genetic disorder caused mainly by PHOX2B mutations and characterized by severe impairment of the autonomic nervous system and central control of breathing. The cardinal feature of CCHS is hypoventilation during sleep and an impaired hypercapnic ventilatory response. This defect has been linked, in part, to anatomical and functional abnormalities of phox2b-expressing neurons in the retrotrapezoid nucleus (RTN), a key component of central CO₂ chemoreception. Although existing mouse models have provided major mechanistic insights, the severe and often perinatal phenotype of several models has limited their use for longer-term therapeutic testing. Here, we generated and characterized, for the first time, a new mouse model bearing the +5 alanine (+5Ala) expansion mutation (phox2b25Ala/+ mice) that reproduces CCHS-like phenotypes described in humans. Phox2b25Ala/+ pups suffered from hypoventilation and had a blunted response to hypercapnia at birth, leading to premature death in 75% of the pups. At the network level, the frequency of inspiratory activity in vitro was significantly reduced in phox2b25Ala/+ mice, and the response to acidosis was affected. At the cellular level, phox2b25Ala/+ mice had a reduced number of phox2b-expressing RTN neurons, with this reduction being less pronounced in the 25% of pups that survived. In conclusion, the +5 alanine expansion that causes CCHS reproduces CCHS-like phenotypes in mice. Phox2b25Ala/+ mice suffer from life-threatening hypoventilation that leads to premature death at birth and a lack of chemosensitivity. However, 25% of phox2b25Ala/+ mice survive until adulthood, representing a valuable opportunity for drug testing in CCHS.

papers.title: MG-STNet: A Compact Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Network for Adaptive Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging from polysomnography (PSG) is a core component of objective sleep analysis and plays a crucial role in enabling reliable clinical assessment and downstream physiological interpretation, yet the non-stationary nature of physiological signals poses significant challenges for compact models with fixed temporal receptive fields that cannot adapt to time-varying sleep rhythms. To address this challenge, we propose MG-STNet, a compact multi-granularity spatiotemporal network for adaptive sleep staging. The model first utilizes a Multi-Granularity Feature Learning Module (MFLM) to extract multi-resolution representations via parallel downsampling branches, thereby reducing sequence length and computational redundancy. Building on this compact representation, the Global-Local Feature Recalibration (GLFR) module recalibrates multi-channel PSG features by jointly leveraging global statistics and local temporal interactions, while the Adaptive Spatiotemporal Convolution (ASTC) module dynamically routes among complementary temporal branches to capture evolving sleep rhythms. Furthermore, a Temporal Attention Encoding Module (TAEM) is integrated to model long-range dependencies within each epoch. We evaluate MG-STNet on Sleep-EDF-20 and Sleep-EDF-78 using subject-independent k-fold cross-validation. The four-channel model achieves accuracies of 87.3% and 84.5% with 46.6K parameters and 17.2M FLOPs, while its single-channel counterpart achieves 86.6% and 83.2% with 48.6K parameters and 9.8M FLOPs. Experimental results indicate that MG-STNet achieves competitive accuracy with a substantially smaller parameter footprint than mainstream deep sleep-staging models, offering a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for automatic sleep staging under computational constraints.

papers.title: GamSleepNet: A Lightweight Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Based on Gabor Feature Extraction and Mamba Sequence Modeling for Single-Channel EEG.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging is a key technology for the precise diagnosis and treatment of sleep disorders and for long-term home sleep monitoring. Due to its convenience of use, single-channel electroencephalogram (EEG) has become a research focus in home sleep monitoring. However, existing algorithms still face several practical bottlenecks. For example, models with a large number of parameters are prone to overfitting on small labeled datasets; the hardware heterogeneity of customized portable sensors makes datasets not directly shareable; large-scale labeled samples are hard to obtain in real scenarios; there is low recognition accuracy for difficult-to-distinguish sleep stages such as N1 and REM; and there is a lack of suitable research methods for evaluating the required scale of training data for lightweight deployment scenarios. In this paper we propose GamSleepNet, a low-parameter-count automatic sleep staging framework for single-channel EEG. The framework combines a feature extraction module (FEB), which integrates improved Gabor kernels with a learnable filter branch, with a standard Mamba selective state-space model (SSM) used for temporal modeling. A teacher-student feature alignment loss (FAL) and a two-stage training strategy are introduced to enhance the discriminative ability for difficult sleep stages. In addition, following the established paradigm of varying the training dataset's size and observing the performance curve, we make four adaptations tailored to sleep staging, thereby determining the appropriate training data volume for GamSleepNet and providing a methodological reference for determining the training data scale required for deploying other models. Under the limited-labeled-subject setting of the Sleep-EDF dataset, the model has 30.86 k parameters and achieves an overall accuracy of 87.86% and a macro F1 score of 82.62%-the highest values among the compared models-and improves the recognition of difficult REM and N1 samples. The model still maintains stable staging performance under low signal-to-noise ratio and label-scarce scenarios.

papers.title: Sleep-Wake Transitions Reveal Distinct Sex-, Race-, Age-, and Sleep State-Specific Electrocardiographic Autonomic Dynamics in Community Adults.
papers.abstract: Sleep comprises one-third of our lives. Autonomic function during sleep is vital for health, yet fundamental population-level information on autonomic changes during sleep-wake transitions remain incompletely characterized. Demographic factors may shape these dynamics in ways not captured during daytime testing. We hypothesized that autonomic changes during sleep-wake transitions differ by demographic group independent of established cardiovascular risk factors. We analyzed 5589 consecutive adults who were in sinus rhythm during overnight home polysomnography in the Sleep Heart Health Study. The ratio of ECG-derived sympathetic-to-parasympathetic (sympathovagal) modulation and EntropyXRR, a nonlinear dynamic measure, was evaluated across 6 sleep-wake stages. Marginal means were estimated for age, sex, and race or ethnicity using mixed-effects models adjusted for cardiovascular risk factors. Interaction terms were used to quantify demographic differences in state-specific autonomic responses. Participants were (median [interquartile range]) 63 [55-72] years old, 53% female, and 15% non-White (9% Black, 6% other races or ethnicities including Hispanic, Asian, and Pacific Islander). Age, sex and race were strongly associated with autonomic changes, but not EntropyXRR, during sleep state transitions independent of cardiovascular risk factors. Sympathovagal modulation: (1) was lowest in female, non-White, and oldest quartile adults; (2) increased transiently during sleep onset for all groups except non-White; and (3) exhibited the largest changes associated with greatest demographic disparities during final morning awakening from sleep. These were driven primarily by changes in vagal modulation. Sleep-wake transitions reveal robust age-, sex-, and race-specific autonomic signatures not apparent during steady-state sleep. This novel foundation may be used to test whether sleep-related autonomic responses contribute unique prognostic value to conventional measures of cardiovascular risk.

papers.title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training.
papers.abstract: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

papers.title: Preconditioning with Menaquinone-7 and Environmental Enrichment Produces Distinct Osteocalcin and Neuroplasticity Responses Following Chronic Social Defeat Stress.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Depression is a growing global health burden, underscoring the need for preventive strategies that complement existing treatments. Environmental enrichment (EE), incorporating physical, cognitive, sensory, and social stimulation, enhances neuroplasticity and stress resilience. Menaquinone-7 (MK-7), a form of vitamin K2, may also support brain health through osteocalcin, a bone-derived hormone involved in cognition and neuroplasticity. This study examined the protective effects of EE and MK-7 preconditioning, alone and combined, against chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), focusing on the osteocalcin-mediated bone-brain axis and structural plasticity. Materials and Methods: Male C57BL/6N mice received MK-7 (100 µg), EE, or both for four weeks before a 10-day CSDS protocol. Depressive-like behavior was assessed using the forced swim and tail suspension tests, while cognition was evaluated using novel object recognition and Y-maze tests. Serum osteocalcin, brain undercarboxylated osteocalcin (ucOC), brain gene expression of Bdnf, Gpr158, and Rbbp4, and protein levels of BDNF, MAP2, and GAP43 were measured. Results: CSDS induced depressive-like behavior and cognitive impairment, accompanied by reductions in serum and brain ucOC, Bdnf expression, BDNF, GAP43, and MAP2. Both MK-7 and EE showed significant main effects on behavioral and cognitive outcomes, while MK-7 exerted broader effects on osteocalcin- and neuroplasticity-related molecular markers. Significant MK-7 × EE interactions were limited to selected outcomes, including FST and brain ucOC, indicating outcome-specific rather than generalized synergy. Conclusions: CSDS disrupts the osteocalcin-mediated bone-brain axis and neuroplasticity-related pathways. MK-7 and EE both improved behavioral and cognitive outcomes, but MK-7 exerted broader effects on ucOC- and BDNF-related molecular markers, whereas their combination produced selective interactions rather than generalized synergy.

papers.title: Operational Definitions of Transition Onset Shape EEG Biomarker Timing in Drowsiness: A Single-Channel Method Comparison.
papers.abstract: Early-warning claims for electroencephalography (EEG)-based drowsiness detection rest on lead times, yet a lead time depends on how onset is operationally defined and is rarely tested against a null. We developed a benchmarking framework and applied it to seven onset estimators and 32 features from single-channel frontal EEG (17 participants, observer-verified drowsiness reports), with external replication in the DROZY dataset (13 sessions with an eligible vigilance-lapse anchor, of 20 retained). Estimator choice shifted onsets by minutes and changed detection coverage from 45% to 100% (Kendall's W = 0.53; external W = 0.71; absolute-agreement intraclass correlation 0.05). In simulation, two-standard-deviation baseline rules flagged onsets in 77-88% of no-change trajectories; null-calibrated thresholds (about 4.6 standard deviations) restored a nominal 5% rate. No estimator showed a statistically detectable excess of onsets in the final 150 s before the anchor relative to spectrum-preserving surrogates, a consensus detector fired before pseudo-anchors as often as before the true anchor, and adding EEG to elapsed session time gave no detectable improvement (area-under-the-curve difference 0.01, 95% confidence interval -0.11 to 0.13). Higuchi fractal dimension and line length correlated weakly with measured electrooculography (|r| ≤ 0.15). We propose interpretability criteria, evidence levels and a reporting checklist for early-onset claims.

papers.title: EEG Theta Power as an Indicator of Cognitive Workload in Student Pilots.
papers.abstract: Aviation operates within a highly cognitively demanding environment, where assessing pilot workload is essential for preventing errors and accidents associated with excessive or insufficient cognitive demand. This study presents a neurophysiological experiment designed to assess pilot brain activity using electroencephalography (EEG) in a high-fidelity Pilatus PC-21 flight simulator. The study focuses on the theta frequency band (4-8 Hz), given its association with mental effort and cognitive engagement. EEG signals were recorded from eight scalp locations in ten pilots during baseline conditions and three flight simulation modules with different levels of task difficulty. Subjective workload was assessed using the NASA-TLX questionnaire, completed after each simulation phase. The results showed higher theta power during the most cognitively demanding flight phase, particularly across frontal, temporal, and occipital regions. papers.title: Neurocognitive and Behavioural Correlates of REM-Predominant Obstructive Sleep Apnoea.
papers.abstract: Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA, REM-OSA) is a phenotype in which obstructive respiratory events occur mainly during REM sleep, and may be associated with distinct daytime consequences. This study investigated the neurocognitive, behavioural, subjective sleep and polysomnographic profile of REM-OSA. Patients were classified as having REM-OSA when the REM Apnoea-Hypopnea Index (AHI)/Non-REM (NREM) AHI ratio was ≥ 2 and were compared with patients whose respiratory events predominantly occurred during NREM sleep (NREM-OSA). Patients evaluated for suspected OSA underwent a neuropsychological battery, including the Mini-Mental State Examination, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test, Digit Span Forward/Backward, Trail Making Test (TMT), Frontal Assessment Battery and Raven's Coloured Progressive Matrices, together with questionnaires evaluating sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index), daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale), impulsivity (Barratt Impulsiveness Scale), anxiety and depression (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale). Of the 91 eligible patients, 17 had mild OSA and were included in sensitivity analyses, while the primary analysis included 74 patients with moderate-to-severe OSA. Thirteen (17.6%) met REM-OSA criteria, and 61 were classified as NREM-OSA. REM-OSA patients had lower overall AHI and oxygen desaturation index and, after False Discovery Rate correction, longer TMT-A, TMT-B and TMT B-A (all q = 0.003). After adjustment for depressive symptoms, REM-OSA independently predicted longer TMT-A (β = 0.298, p = 0.002), TMT-B (β = 0.235, p = 0.016), TMT B-A (β = 0.258, p = 0.018) and higher impulsivity (β = 0.237, p = 0.043), but not global PSQI scores (β = 0.210, p = 0.086). Sensitivity analyses confirmed poorer TMT-A performance in REM-OSA. These results highlight the neurocognitive relevance of REM phenotype despite lower overall respiratory severity.

papers.title: Strategies to establish a biologically defined Parkinson's disease cohort prior to the onset of clinically significant motor symptoms.
papers.abstract: Identifying individuals at risk for neurodegeneration is a priority for clinical trials. Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) deploys strategies to enroll individuals before typical clinical Parkinson's disease symptoms: recruiting polysomnogram-confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and central identification of hyposmia via smell testing. Groups were divided into RBD with and without hyposmia (RBD+Hyposmia, RBD-Hyposmia) and hyposmia with and without self-reported dream enactment behavior (Hyposmia + DEB, Hyposmia-DEB). Participants underwent clinical and biomarker testing including CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (CSFaSynSAA) and dopamine transporter imaging. While all enrollment strategies showed robust enrichment for CSFaSynSAA positivity, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia + DEB were more likely CSFaSynSAA+ (94% and 85%) vs RBD-Hyposmia (40%) and Hyposmia-DEB (55%). Among CSFaSynSAA+, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia + DEB had more mood, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms than Hyposmia-DEB. PPMI identified a large biologically-defined early neuronal synucleinopathy cohort and demonstrated biomarker and multi-domain clinical heterogeneity within CSFaSynSAA+ individuals prior to symptom onset.

papers.title: Objective-to-Subjective Sleep Discrepancy in Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Pilot EEG Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep disturbance is common in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), but the relationship between subjectively perceived and objectively measured sleep duration remains poorly understood. This pilot study aimed to compare objective and subjective total sleep time (TST) and to explore clinical factors associated with each measure and the difference between them. It also examined the relationship between this difference and nocturnal blood pressure regulation. Materials and Methods: Twenty-two hospitalized patients with RA underwent overnight sleep monitoring using a portable single-channel electroencephalography (EEG) device and provided subjective estimates of TST for the same night in response to a question asked the following morning. Sleep discrepancy was defined as subjective minus EEG-derived TST. Associations with clinical variables were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation analysis with false discovery rate correction. Exploratory regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index were performed. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was available for 20 patients. Results: Subjective TST exceeded EEG-derived TST by a median of 82.75 min (p = 0.0008), and the two measurements were not significantly correlated (ρ = 0.119, p = 0.598). A more positive signed sleep discrepancy was associated with lower serum albumin (ρ = -0.723, q = 0.0020), higher C-reactive protein (CRP) levels (ρ = 0.624, q = 0.0134), glucocorticoid use (q = 0.0462), higher DAS28-CRP (q = 0.0495), and greater functional disability (q = 0.0495). Associations with albumin and CRP persisted in separate exploratory models adjusted for age, sex, and body mass index. Patients with a conventional dipper blood pressure (BP) pattern had a lower signed sleep discrepancy than those with other nocturnal BP patterns (p = 0.0087). Conclusions: In this small exploratory study, subjective sleep duration in patients with RA was generally longer than EEG-derived sleep duration. Furthermore, preliminary associations were observed between sleep discrepancy and inflammatory and clinical characteristics, as well as with nocturnal BP patterns. These findings require confirmation in larger studies, and the clinical significance of sleep discrepancy remains uncertain.

papers.title: Exploratory observations of sleep during contest preparation in a natural bodybuilder: a case study.
papers.abstract: Natural bodybuilders undergo prolonged caloric restriction combined with high training volumes in the lead-up to competitions to achieve extremely low body fat levels while preserving lean mass. Although sleep plays a critical role in recovery and metabolic regulation, its response to contest preparation remains under-explored. This case study followed a 24-year-old male natural bodybuilder across four months: off-season (AS-1) and a three-month contest preparation phase (AS-2 to AS-5). Body composition, energy status and sleep were assessed. The athlete lost 5.7 kg (6.6%) of initial body mass, including approximately 4.0 kg of estimated fat mass, reaching an estimated body fat percentage of 5.4% two weeks before competition. Energy intake dropped from 4345 to 2080 kcal per day, shifting energy balance from a 1159 kcal surplus at AS-1 to a 1052 kcal deficit at AS-5. Estimated energy availability progressively declined, reaching 23.9 kcal·kg FFM-1·day-1 at AS-5, below a proposed male-specific threshold for potentially low energy availability. Sleep quality deteriorated markedly: sleep efficiency declined from 93% to 83%, wake after sleep onset nearly tripled, and rapid eye movement sleep dropped from 30.8% to 4.4% at AS-4 and 12% at AS-5. Hypnograms showed sleep fragmentation and impaired REM transition. These findings suggest that sleep characteristics may vary during periods of severe energy deficit in bodybuilding contest preparation.

papers.title: Visual function and circadian rest-activity rhythms in US older adults: The National Health and Aging Trends Study.
papers.abstract: To evaluate associations of visual function with accelerometer-derived rest-activity rhythm (RAR) metrics and 24-hour continuous activity patterns among older adults. We analyzed data from 728 U.S. Medicare beneficiaries (weighted mean age 79.1±6.0 years, 78% White, 56% female) who completed objective vision assessments and provided ≥ 3 days of accelerometer data in NHATS Round 11 (2021). Visual functions included distance acuity, near acuity, and contrast sensitivity. Wrist-worn accelerometer data were used to derive parametric RAR metrics (amplitude, mesor, acrophase, alpha, beta, and percent rhythm) and nonparametric RAR metrics (relative amplitude, intradaily variability [IV], interdaily stability [IS]). Associations were examined using weighted linear regression and function-on-scalar regression (FOSR). Poorer visual function, regardless of type, was associated with lower amplitude (rhythm strength, both parametric and non-parametric metrics) and lower percent rhythm (rhythmicity), but not with mesor (average activity level), acrophase (peak activity timing), or alpha (peak-trough width). Distance acuity showed a statistically significant nonlinear association with IS. We did not observe any statistically significant associations for beta and IV after type 1 error correction. FOSR showed lower daytime activity and higher nighttime activity during typical sleep hours among those with vision impairment, with simultaneous significance limited to a small portion of the day. Findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Worse visual function was associated with weaker and less robust circadian RARs in a representative sample of older adults. Longitudinal and mechanistic studies are warranted to understand the intertwined relationships between visual function and circadian health.

papers.title: The circadian gene Nr1d1 regulates female luteinization via the NF-κB pathway.
papers.abstract: Luteinization is essential for luteal function. Progesterone secreted by the corpus luteum is critical for pregnancy. Evidence indicates that the circadian clock regulates luteinization; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. To investigate the effects of circadian rhythm disruption on luteinization, a constant-light-exposure mouse model was established. In vitro luteinization models using mouse ovarian granulosa cells and KGN cells were employed to investigate the specific circadian clock effector Nr1d1 and its regulatory mechanisms. In mice, constant light exposure was associated with altered expression of ovarian circadian clock genes and enhanced luteinization-associated responses. In mouse granulosa cells, Bmal1 knockdown caused circadian rhythm disturbances, reduced luteinization-related gene expression, and resulted in luteinization failure and decreased progesterone secretion. In KGN cells, the Nr1d1 agonist SR9009 promoted luteinization-related gene expression, enhanced luteinization, and increased progesterone secretion. Conversely, treatment with the Nr1d1 inhibitor SR8278 or si-Nr1d1 in KGN cells yielded opposite effects. In KGN cells, LPS-mediated activation of the NF-κB pathway induced luteinization failure and decreased progesterone secretion. In contrast, co-treatment with SR9009 and LPS reduced NF-κB pathway activity, enhanced luteinization, and increased progesterone secretion. Collectively, these findings indicate that the circadian clock gene Nr1d1 facilitates luteinization potentially through suppressing the NF-κB pathway.

papers.title: Acute Effects of Prolonged Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation on Cortical Excitability: A Randomized Crossover TMS-EEG Study
papers.abstract: Background: prolonged intermittent theta burst stimulation (piTBS), as used in Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), achieves antidepressant efficacy, yet its acute single-session mechanisms remain elusive. EEG can capture online oscillatory dynamics during piTBS and pre- to post-stimulation changes in TMS-evoked cortical reactivity. Methods: in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial, 40 healthy males completed two visits ( [≥]7-day washout), receiving active or sham piTBS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Inter-train EEG power was analyzed across three blocks of 20 trains in 37 participants. Pre- and post-stimulation measures of TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), working memory and sustained attention were analyzed in all 40 participants. Results: left frontal theta power followed different trajectories across blocks during active and sham piTBS (conditionxblock interaction, p = .014). During active piTBS, theta power was below baseline in blocks 1 and 2 and increased significantly from block 2 to block 3. Across conditions, alpha power was lower in blocks 2 and 3 than in block 1. Direct comparison of pre-to-post TEP changes between active and sham piTBS identified no significant clusters in the N45, P60, N100 and P180 component windows. Exploratory analyses within active piTBS identified a decrease in frontal N100 cluster amplitude and an increase in posterior N100 cluster amplitude. Neither behavioral outcome showed condition-dependent changes. Conclusion: a single session of active piTBS modulated left frontal theta power between stimulation trains. Whether this early response is associated with cumulative plasticity or antidepressant outcomes following SNT warrants further investigation.

papers.title: Quantitative EEG Differences Across Two Sedation Conditions in a Child with Epilepsy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Sedation is frequently required to obtain electroencephalography (EEG) recordings in children with neurodevelopmental disorders and structural etiologies of epilepsy. However, the extent to which different sedative agents influence quantitative interictal epileptiform discharge (IED) burden remains insufficiently characterized. A child with congenital cytomegalovirus-associated structural brain injury underwent EEG recordings under two sedation conditions: continuous low-dose propofol infusion and oral chloral hydrate. Quantitative analyses were performed using a duration-matched, within-subject design. Artifact-minimized EEG segments of equal duration (15.52 min) were analyzed. IED burden was quantified using spike frequency (spikes/min) and spike index (percentage of 10 s epochs containing ≥1 spike). Spectral power distribution and spectral edge frequency (SEF95) were also evaluated. The chloral hydrate recording showed a higher observed spike frequency than the propofol recording (14.11 vs. 4.12 spikes/min; descriptive rate ratio, 3.42) and a higher 10-s spike index (84.95% vs. 27.96%). Spectral analysis demonstrated lower SEF95 and greater delta predominance in the propofol recording, whereas the chloral hydrate recording showed relatively greater theta-alpha activity. However, because they were obtained approximately one year apart and under different clinical circumstances, including intercurrent illness during the chloral hydrate recording, these differences cannot be attributed specifically to the sedative agents. This case illustrates the importance of considering sedation, clinical context, and vigilance state when longitudinally interpreting quantitative pediatric EEG findings.

papers.title: Guipi Tang Combined with Probiotics Ameliorates Sleep Deprivation-Induced Hippocampal Injury and Pentobarbital-Induced Sleep Alterations in Mice.

Furthermore, serum levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α (tumor necrosis factor-alpha) and IL-1β (interleukin-1 beta) differed significantly among groups (n = 5 per group; F (4,20) = 3.959, p = 0.0159 and F (4,20) = 10.26, p = 0.0001, respectively). Hippocampal metabolic profiles were characterized using untargeted metabolomics. Intrinsic interactions among behavioral, immune, and metabolic indices were evaluated through correlation analysis. The functional pathways associated with the differential metabolites were determined using the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis. CSD mice exhibited typical anxiety-like behaviors, characterized by reduced time spent in the central area in the OFT and fewer entries into that area, as well as increased latency to enter the open arms in the EPM test. papers.title: Scalp EEG seizure warning in children under a pre-specified, locked evaluation: confound audit, structured chance levels and a negative result

Reported performance of scalp electroencephalographic (EEG) seizure prediction is often inflated by lenient evaluation and by the vigilance-state, clock-time and admission-trend structure of monitoring data. A statistical-process-control warning method was evaluated under a written protocol, then re-designed as a state-conditioned, directional scheme on seven global EEG features, frozen with a hash-recorded configuration and time-stamped pre-specification, assessed by nested leave-one-patient-out cross-validation, and applied once to two validation cohorts (a second batch from the same unit and the public CHB-MIT database from Children's Hospital Boston; 101 evaluable seizures). Main results. The original method detected 44% of evaluable seizures at 0.48 false alarms per hour, no better than a random predictor (51%, p = 0.86); its statistic moved three times more with vigilance state than with seizure approach. The frozen scheme detected 15 of 45 development seizures (33%) at 0.47 false alarms per hour, above analytic (21%, p = 0.034) and permutation chance, but a predictor using only clock time, vigilance state and days since admission reproduced most of this, and the signal was confined to the last 30 min. In validation it detected 19 seizures (19%) at 0.60 false alarms per hour against 26% chance (p = 0.96); no secondary endpoint was met, and with the child as the unit of analysis no cohort was above chance. In Case 3, a 52-year-old male with worsening episodic déjà vu exhibited focal interictal rhythmic activity, providing objective data to guide shared decision-making and successful initiation of antiseizure treatment. Extended-duration remote EEG monitoring bridges key diagnostic gaps by offering flexible, real-world data collection over extended timeframes (up to 30 days). papers.abstract: BackgroundComparative evidence regarding the immediate subjective and physiological responses to conventional suction-type and wearable conductive silicone silver spike point (SSP) electrodes remains limited.ObjectiveTo compare responses to conventional SSP stimulation at V1-associated sites and wearable silicone SSP stimulation at V3-associated sites with a nonequivalent no-current control.MethodsFifty-four healthy young adults were randomized to control, conventional SSP, or silicone SSP groups (18 per group). Conventional electrodes were applied without current in the control group, whereas both active groups received 20 min of stimulation. The primary outcome was pre-to-post change in the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS). Exploratory secondary outcomes included electroencephalography (EEG), heart rate variability (HRV), and masseter electromyography (EMG). Analyses included mixed repeated-measures ANOVA and Welch ANOVA with Dunnett T3-adjusted comparisons.ResultsA significant time × group interaction was observed for KSS [F(2, 51) = 4.693, p = .013, partial η2 = .155]. Mean ± SD changes were 0.53 ± 1.77, 1.14 ± 1.95, and 2.92 ± 3.28 points in the control, conventional SSP, and silicone SSP groups, respectively. Post hoc analysis showed a significant difference between the silicone SSP and control groups (mean difference, 2.389; 95% CI, 0.154-4.624; adjusted p = .034), but not between the two active stimulation groups (adjusted p = .162). No significant time × group interactions were observed for EEG, HRV, or EMG.ConclusionKSS changes differed between silicone SSP and no-current control, but superiority or equivalence relative to conventional SSP was not established. The simultaneous differences in stimulation site and electrode design prevent attribution of the observed findings to either factor independently.

papers.title: Cognition in 6-17-year-olds with Generalized and Focal Pharmaco-responsive Non-structural Epilepsies and its Correlates on Diffusion Tensor Imaging and Quantitative EEG: A Comparative Observational Study.
papers.abstract: The study compares cognition and its correlates on diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and quantitative electroencephalogram (qEEG) between generalized and focal pharmaco-responsive non-structural epilepsies and evaluates behavioral comorbidities. The study was conducted in a tertiary care teaching hospital in north India in 20 generalized and 30 focal pharmaco-responsive non-structural epilepsies in 6- to 17-year-olds. Cognition was tested using Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-IV (WISC-IV) and Stroop test and behavior was evaluated using Childhood Behavior Checklist (CBCL). All the cases underwent DTI and a subset underwent resting and task-based qEEG evaluation. Cognition scores were comparable between generalized and focal epilepsies; however, both showed significant impairment compared with historical controls. On DTI, fractional anisotropy of corpus callosum (body in focal and splenium in generalized) and cingulate cortex (in both) correlated significantly with cognition scores. On resting qEEG, cognition scores correlated negatively with absolute α, δ (focal epilepsy), β and θ powers (generalized epilepsy), and positively with α and δ powers (generalized epilepsy). Performance on task-based qEEG showed negative correlation with absolute delta power in both. Impaired CBCL scores were seen in 25% generalized and 16.7% focal epilepsies. Similar correlates on DTI and qEEG for generalized and focal epilepsies highlight the effect of network model of epilepsy on cognition. The negative correlation of α and β powers with WISC-IV and Stroop scores probably indicates an underlying anxious, tensed, and inattentive state leading to impaired performance in these tests. These cases should be routinely screened for behavioral comorbidities providing a therapeutic target for cognition.

papers.title: Electroacupuncture Ameliorates Circadian Rhythm Disruption-Induced Oligoasthenospermia in Mice by Modulating the Sirt1/Nrf2 Antioxidant Signaling Pathway.
papers.abstract: The growing prevalence of shift work and nocturnal light exposure in modern lifestyles has made circadian disruption an underrecognized environmental risk factor for male oligoasthenospermia. The core molecular network underlying circadian disruption-induced spermatogenic impairment remains incompletely understood, and targeted non-pharmacological interventions are limited. This study sought to identify candidate regulatory targets for circadian disruption-related oligoasthenospermia and investigate the protective mechanism of electroacupuncture. Gene sets associated with circadian rhythm and oligoasthenospermia were retrieved from GeneCards, OMIM, and GEO databases. Candidate hub genes and pathways were screened via intersection analysis, functional enrichment, and seven machine learning algorithms. A chronic jet lag mouse model was established and randomly divided into control, circadian disruption, and electroacupuncture groups. Sperm parameters, serum reproductive hormone levels, testicular and hepatic clock gene expression, testicular histology, oxidative stress status, and Sirt1/Nrf2 pathway activity were assessed. Five hub genes linked to both circadian rhythm and oligoasthenospermia (IL1B, NFE2L2, PCNA, DMPK, MYH9) were identified, with functional enrichment highlighting pathways related to oxidative stress, gonadal development, and hormone regulation. In vivo, circadian disruption impaired sperm quality, dysregulated reproductive hormones, downregulated testicular clock genes, disrupted spermatogenic structure, elevated testicular oxidative stress, and suppressed the Sirt1/Nrf2 pathway. Electroacupuncture effectively reversed these pathological changes, restored hepatic clock rhythmicity, and upregulated key molecules of the testicular Sirt1/Nrf2 antioxidant pathway. Electroacupuncture ameliorates circadian disruption-induced spermatogenic impairment in mice. This protective effect is associated with the restoration of peripheral circadian rhythm and activation of the testicular Sirt1/Nrf2 antioxidant pathway.

papers.title: Circadian Rhythms, Exercise, and Metabolic Remodeling in MASLD: From Chronometabolism to Muscle-Preserving Care.
papers.abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) links hepatic lipid accumulation with insulin resistance, disturbed sleep, and impaired muscle health. This critical narrative review integrates clinical, metabolomics, and mechanistic evidence identified through a structured multi-database search and citation-tracing workflow covering PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar to 30 September 2026, focusing on circadian regulation, exercise, and muscle-preserving care. Hepatic clocks coordinate nutrient handling, bile-acid signaling, mitochondrial metabolism, and redox balance. Sleep and meal-timing disruption are associated with adverse metabolic phenotypes, although MASLD-specific causal evidence remains limited. Exercise improves liver and metabolic outcomes, but no universal optimal session time has been established. Time-restricted eating should be evaluated alongside energy intake, diet quality, protein distribution, sleep, and adherence. Complex lipids, acylcarnitines, bile acids, ketone bodies, and amino acids offer complementary research signals; their interpretation requires standardized sampling, analytical quality control, and external validation. Circulating concentrations should not be equated with tissue flux or treatment benefit. Clinical care should integrate fibrosis and cardiometabolic risk assessment with sustainable weight management, progressive resistance and aerobic exercise, adequate protein, and sleep assessment. Future trials should pair repeated, timed metabolite measurements with liver, body-composition, strength, and physical-function outcomes to establish whether these signatures improve clinical decisions.

papers.title: EEG morphology and peri-ictal MRI abnormalities in status epilepticus and ictal-interictal continuum.
papers.abstract: Status epilepticus (SE) is a neurological emergency that may have long-term consequences. Peri-ictal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) abnormalities (PMAs) may serve as marker of potential acute ictal brain injury and can be used for estimating the risk of SE-defining electroencephalography (EEG) patterns. We hypothesized that excitatory-predominant EEG morphologies reflect higher metabolic demand and a greater likelihood of PMAs than inhibitory-predominant morphologies. In this single-center prospective cohort (February 2019-April 2025), we included patients who had either SE or ictal-interictal continuum (IIC) reported on EEG and underwent acute magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (≤48 h). Excitatory-predominant morphology was defined by a sharp-wave amplitude greater than those of the positive and slow wave, a broad sharp wave (>200 ms), or superimposed fast activity. Inhibitory-predominant morphology was defined by the positive or slow-wave amplitude greater than that of a sharp wave. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated the association between EEG morphology and PMAs on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR). Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho assessed correlations between the number of excitatory features (0-2) and MRI sequences showing PMAs (none, arterial spin labeling [ASL] hyperperfusion only, or DWI/FLAIR). Among 205 included patients (134 IIC, 71 SE), excitatory-predominant patterns and lateralized periodic discharges were associated with increased risk of DWI/FLAIR PMAs (p = .001 and p = .02, respectively). In IIC patients, excitatory-predominant morphology was the only predictor of PMAs (p = .002). In the subset with ASL, DWI, and FLAIR sequences (n = 145), the number of excitatory features correlated strongly with types of sequences affected by PMAs (Kendall's tau p < .001; Spearman's rho p < .001). Excitatory-predominant morphology, as opposed to inhibitory-predominant patterns, was associated with a more frequent occurrence of PMAs. These findings support an EEG morphology framework based on excitatory-inhibitory balance across IIC and SE.

papers.title: From hemodynamics to function: the role of fNIRS and hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems in next-generation assistive technologies for rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Assistive technologies (AT) serve as fundamental tools for rehabilitation because they help people with neurological or physical disabilities to restore their abilities, independence and their overall life satisfaction. Existing AT control methods, which include manual operation, eye tracking, voice commands, electromyography (EMG) and electroencephalography (EEG), have improved rehabilitation results but still face challenges because of their inability to maintain reliable performance during user exhaustion and difficulties operating in challenging situations. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) has recently become a new neuroimaging technique that provides excellent imaging capability, can be used while moving, and has portable design features. fNIRS-based devices such as wheelchairs, robotic prostheses, and brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have proven their ability to decode user intention and assist rehabilitation. The limited ability of fNIRS to measure time intervals prevents its use in real-time systems. The hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems combine EEG technology, which provides high-speed temporal measurements, with fNIRS technology, which provides spatial and hemodynamic measurements. The multimodal techniques combine different measurement methods, which improve accuracy while decreasing false positive results and increasing system adaptability. This review critically examines how AT control modalities have been evolving, and it also measures what fNIRS can do technically, plus what it struggles with, and then it pulls together the available evidence on hybrid EEG-fNIRS systems as a possible way toward more adaptive, user-centered rehabilitation technologies.

papers.title: Emotional challenges and coping strategies in the transition to fatherhood: perspectives of new fathers and health professionals: a qualitative study.
papers.abstract: Fathers' needs are often overlooked in perinatal care. This study explored the emotional, practical, and relational challenges of transitioning to fatherhood and identified opportunities for digital support.We interviewed expectant and new fathers and health professionals working in perinatal care. Fathers discussed their emotional experiences, daily challenges, coping strategies, and interactions with healthcare services. Health professionals described existing support and gaps in care. We used thematic analysis to identify patterns across both groups. Fathers described worry, anxiety, frustration, and helplessness associated with sleep deprivation, changing relationships, work pressures, and uncertainty about caregiving. Many felt excluded from antenatal education and unsure how to support a partner experiencing emotional distress. Mother-centred care, limited involvement in appointments, and stigma around expressing emotions made it harder for fathers to seek help. Health professionals identified gaps in support and opportunities to involve fathers more actively in perinatal care.Fathers wanted to be involved and confident in caregiving, yet uncertainty about their role, exclusion from care, and social expectations that discourage vulnerability shaped their experiences of distress. The findings highlight the need for father-inclusive perinatal care and accessible digital tools that offer practical guidance, emotional support, and opportunities for connection. Further research with more diverse groups of fathers could inform the development of equitable and responsive interventions.

papers.title: Identification of Hypoxia- and Circadian Rhythm-Related Prognostic Genes in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Through Integrative Transcriptomic and Single-Cell Analysis.
papers.abstract: Hypoxia perturbs circadian rhythm gene expression in hepatocellular carcinoma, yet prognostic genes associated with both processes remain insufficiently characterized. Data from the liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) cohort in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were analyzed. Candidate genes were identified by intersecting differentially expressed genes (DEGs) with 27 hypoxia- and circadian rhythm-related genes and were further refined using univariate Cox regression and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression; a random survival forest (RSF) risk model was then constructed and validated. Independent prognostic and functional enrichment analyses, immune infiltration profiling, single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), and immunohistochemistry (IHC) were subsequently performed. Four prognostic genes (ADM, PFKFB3, SERPINE1, and RORA) were identified through integrative computational analysis. The RSF model stratified LIHC patients into the high-risk group (HRG) and the low-risk group (LRG), which had significantly different survival outcomes, and the risk score and tumor stage were combined in a nomogram. The four genes were co-enriched in four pathways; eight immune cell types, including natural killer T (NKT) cells, differed between the risk groups. scRNA-seq identified stem-like/hypoxic malignant cells whose differentiation trajectory showed distinct expression dynamics of the four genes. IHC confirmed significantly higher ADM and PFKFB3 protein expression in LIHC tissues, whereas protein-level evidence for SERPINE1 and RORA was inconclusive. These findings support further prognostic evaluation of LIHC and investigation of the links among hypoxia, metabolic reprogramming, and stemness.

papers.title: Physiologically Based Pharmacokinetic Modeling of Acoziborole Supplements Clinical Drug-Drug Interaction Data and Predicts Time-dependent Interaction Duration Following Single-Dose Oral Treatment for African Sleeping Sickness
papers.abstract: Acoziborole is a novel single-dose oral treatment for gambiense human African trypanosomiasis (g-HAT). Acoziborole's long half-life and complex, time-dependent effects on drug-metabolizing enzymes necessitate drug-drug interaction (DDI) assessment. A physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model was developed to characterize acoziborole DDI potential in African patients with g-HAT and support product labeling recommendations. Model development used available physicochemical, in vitro binding and interaction parameters, and clinical pharmacokinetic data from healthy participants and participants with g-HAT. Clinical DDI data for cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 and CYP2D6 substrates were used to assess and refine the PBPK model. Predicted PK was validated using independent clinical datasets. The model was applied to predict clinically untested scenarios, including time-dependent DDI with CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 probe substrates, and DDIs with CYP1A2, CYP2B6, CYP2C8, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, and BCRP substrates. The model adequately described acoziborole PK in healthy participants and participants with g-HAT. Simulations predicted strong CYP3A4 induction to ~4 weeks, then moderate to ~9 weeks and CYP2D6 clinically relevant inhibition for up to 3 months post-acoziborole administration. Clinically relevant exposure reductions were predicted for concomitantly administered CYP3A4 substrates, particularly during the first month post-acoziborole. Prolonged and clinically relevant exposure increases in sensitive CYP2D6 substrates were predicted, although DDI risk was lower and shorter for CYP2D6 substrates also metabolized by CYP3A4. Simulated interactions with other enzymes were weak-to-moderate, with minimal transporter-mediated effects. The findings supported discussions with regulatory agencies to inform duration-based risk management strategies and prescribing information for acoziborole, and co-administration with common medications in the target population.

papers.title: Depression is associated with endometrial polyp occurrence and convergent gut microbiota-mitochondrial alterations: a multi-omics case-control study.
papers.abstract: Endometrial polyps (EPs) affect 7.8%-34.9% of women and cause abnormal uterine bleeding and reproductive failure, yet their pathogenesis is unclear. Depression is over-represented among women with EPs but is usually read as reactive distress; whether that association involves the gut microbiota and mitochondrial biology is unknown. We combined a hospital-based case-control analysis (n = 466), faecal full-length 16S rRNA and blood leukocyte RNA-seq in 30 participants (PD n = 11, PND n = 12, NPND n = 7), and a chronic restraint stress (CRS) mouse model with bacterial supplementation. Depression was significantly associated with higher odds of EP in the full cohort (unadjusted OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.55-3.34; P < 0.001), and this trend remained stable following confounder adjustment, propensity-score matching and multiple sensitivity analyses. Signals were partitioned into EP-specific, depression-specific and dual-associated classes. In the EP-specific class, predicted microbial functions showed less electron-transfer gene content (complexes I-II), while host ETC subunits spanning complexes I, III and IV (NDUFA1, UQCRH, COX6B1, COX7A2) were coordinately downregulated and CCR2, CCR5 and UMPS upregulated, with enrichment for oxidative phosphorylation. Dual-associated signals comprised higher Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and lower Eggerthella lenta, negatively correlated (Kendall τ = -0.37, P = 0.007; PD > PND > NPND), together with downregulation of GDF15, HIC1, TCF7L2 and ICAM1. In mice, restraint stress was accompanied by stromal proliferation exceeding that in estradiol-treated controls and by reduced uterine TOMM20; oral F. prausnitzii given after stress was associated with higher TOMM20 and lower proliferation, whereas E. lenta was not. These findings place a convergent gut microbiota-mitochondrial axis at the intersection of depression and endometrial proliferation, and nominate candidate taxa and transcripts for hypothesis-driven validation. Limitations: multi-omics profiling included 30 participants (11, 12 and 7) with no depression-only cell; microbial functions were predicted by PICRUSt2 and no metabolite was measured; medication use, diet, physical activity, sleep and hormonal status were incompletely captured; and each bacterial group contained three animals. The axis proposed here is therefore hypothesis-generating and requires longitudinal, metabolomic and tissue-specific validation.
